newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Golkar assured of victory in election.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Golkar assured of victory in election.

text.p: Indonesia opens its general election campaign on Sunday with the ruling Golkar assured of victory after three decades in power.

Political attention is focused not so much on the May 29 elections for the 500-seat House of Representatives, but on a presidential poll in March next year and the possible running mate for President Suharto.

"I think most people feel that this election is not particularly interesting because there is nothing new in the process," analyst Mari Pangistu of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Jakarta told Reuters.
Golkar, in power during the whole of Suharto's 30-year rule, will be trying to edge its share of the popular vote over 70 percent after registering 68 percent in the last polls in 1992.

Of the two other parties allowed to contest the national and local polls, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) won 17 percent last time and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) 15 percent.
"People are not worried about the outcome of the election. They are more worried about the possibility of destabilising events in the month leading up to the election," Pangistu said.
"Everyone is looking towards the presidential elections next year," another analyst commented.

Economic analysts say the election is unlikely to damage investor confidence in Indonesia, but there are jitters in the money market over the potential for trouble and banking sources say some short-term money has sought safe haven elsewhere. The rupiah also hit a historic low against the dollar during the day before, recovering slightly.
Political analysts say a more important element affecting investment is President Suharto's future and a possible successor to the 75-year-old leader.
Suharto has presided over massive growth in the Indonesian economy, where per capita income has more than doubled in the last decade to more than $1,100.
He is widely expected to seek a seventh five-year term in office in March next year. But so far no potential successor has clearly emerged, despite questions over his age and health.
If the current campaign lacks excitement, some political analysts say the jockeying for position could provide some indication of the country's political future.

Bruce Gale, regional manager of the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy in Singapore, said the way Golkar performs could give pointers to the strengths of vice-presidential contenders.

Constitutionally, if Suharto died the vice-president would take over as acting president for the remainder of the term. Given the president's age, the next vice-president could also be seen as a potential successor should Suharto retire.
Current Vice-President Try Sutrisno is highly regarded, but a vice-president has never before served more than one term.
Indonesian sources say there is popular uneasiness with the country moving into uncharted waters over the succession issue.
Central Java, the most populous area in the sprawling nation of 200 million people, has been hit by election-connected violence in recent weeks.

A "battle of the colours" has erupted between supporters of Golkar and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), with yellow and green banners representing the two parties respectively springing up across the countryside.
Political observers say the violence so far has been localised and almost along "tribal" lines.

The government has banned parades and rallies to try to prevent the violence of past campaigns and security forces have pledged to maintain order. The parties have also agreed that no two groups should campaign in the same area at the same time.

Some 125 million people are eligible to vote under a system of proportional representation for the 425 elected seats in the assembly. The other 75 seats will be filled by the military, whose members do not vote.
